children.text: New Census Bureau data showed Latino/a population growth at three times the national average. By 1996, Hispanics were projected to add more people to the U.S. population than any other ethnic group, and in the early 21st century, they would grow by 1 million per year, placing them on track to become the second-largest ethnic group behind African Americans. The Congressional Hispanic Caucus proposed major bilingual education reform that would concentrate funding on low-income areas with large numbers of limited-English-proficient students. A coalition of over 20 Latino/a organizations called on Congress to stop what they described as racist rhetoric in the NAFTA debate, citing floor speeches in which representatives described Mexico as a source of heroin, baseball players, and a pigpen. Analysts from the National Council of La Raza compared the rhetoric to historical slurs against Jewish and Black Americans. In Los Angeles, a wave of drive-by shootings reportedly tapered off after leaders of the Mexican Mafia prison gang ordered street gangs to stop the violence. San Diego County voted to bill the federal government for the cost of services to undocumented residents, and a school board in Vista, California, passed a resolution criticizing federal laws requiring schools to educate all children regardless of citizenship. The Clinton administration reached an agreement with Cuba to repatriate 1,500 Cuban nationals held in federal prisons who arrived during the 1980 Mariel exodus, raising concerns among Cuban Americans about broader concessions to the Castro government.

Correspondent Patricia Guadalupe reported on a bill introduced by California Congressman Xavier Becerra to create an independent commission to investigate Border Patrol abuses. According to the human rights group America's Watch, abuse cases along the U.S.-Mexico border had risen sharply. Becerra's proposed commission would have subpoena power, enforcement authority, and community outreach capacity. The INS opposed the bill as redundant and costly, arguing its own proposed citizens' advisory panel could handle abuse complaints. Becerra countered that an advisory panel without investigative or disciplinary powers was insufficient and that the current complaint system was slow, underfunded, and rarely resulted in accountability.
The US Hispanic Chamber of Commerce Convention

Latino USA's Maria Martin reported from the 14th Annual Convention of the US Hispanic Chamber of Commerce in New York City, where over 600 exhibitors represented corporate America's growing interest in the Latino market. With an estimated $185 billion in combined purchasing power among the country's 25 million Latinos, major brands including Pepsi, Coca-Cola, Sprint, AT&T, Nabisco, and JCPenney were actively courting Hispanic consumers. Goya Foods, the largest Latino-owned business with $450 million in revenue, and Café Bustelo were both expanding into new product categories and markets. The convention adopted resolutions supporting NAFTA and calling for greater Latino/a representation on corporate boards, where Latino/as held fewer than one-third of one percent of Fortune 500 seats. Chamber president Jose Nino reflected on the organization's growth from a 1979 gathering in a high school gymnasium with 250,000 Hispanic-owned businesses to a major convention representing 650,000 such enterprises.

Correspondent Mandalit del Barco reported from both New York and San Juan on the upcoming dual votes on Puerto Rico's political status. In New York, an unofficial plebiscite was scheduled for October 7 through 9, open to island-born residents and their voting-age children on the mainland. On the island, a formal vote was set for November, though island officials had excluded mainland Puerto Ricans from participating. City Council member Victor Robles defended the New York vote as an expression of identity regardless of geography. In San Juan, opinions were sharply divided. Some residents felt those who had left the island had no standing to weigh in, while others argued Puerto Ricans on the mainland had lived the reality of statehood firsthand and thus had unique insight. Archeologist Dr. Ricardo Alegria strongly opposed statehood, arguing it would end Puerto Rico's nationality and culture, and said that pro-statehood television ads depicting stacks of dollars were misleading to residents who had never experienced poverty in a U.S. city. A street musician living with AIDS said the government had never helped him, and he saw no reason to vote.

The Smithsonian Institution dedicated its Hispanic Heritage Month commemoration to the memory of Cesar Chavez, who had died the previous April. A tribute event featured a screening of the documentary Si Se Puede and remarks by Dolores Huerta, co-founder and first vice president of the United Farm Workers. Huerta described Chavez as a self-educated man with only an eighth-grade education who succeeded where every previous effort to organize farmworkers had failed. She noted that conditions for farmworkers in Arizona remained dire, with workers going unpaid, and said Chavez's spirit now accompanied the movement everywhere rather than being confined to a single place. A black jacket bearing the red UFW eagle that Chavez wore was on display at the Smithsonian Museum of American History.
